message.content:
**First Studio Ghibli film to win the Japan Academy Film Prize for Picture of the Year**

| Year | Film | Notes |
|------|------|-------|
| **1997** | *Princess Mononoke* (宮崎駿／スタジオジブリ) | Won “Picture of the Year” at the 20th Japan Academy Prize. It was the first Ghibli feature to receive this top honor. |

> *Princess Mononoke* was released in Japan on July 12, 1997. It became the highest‑grossing Japanese film of the decade, selling roughly **1.5 million tickets** and earning about **¥1.2 billion** (≈ US$12 million) domestically. Worldwide, it grossed around **US$15 million**.

---

### How its box‑office success boosted Ghibli’s international popularity

| Aspect | Impact |
|--------|--------|
| **Domestic record‑breaking revenue** | Demonstrated that Ghibli could produce a blockbuster that resonated with mainstream audiences, proving the viability of large‑budget, high‑quality anime for global markets. |
| **Critical acclaim & awards** | Winning Picture of the Year and receiving numerous domestic accolades positioned Ghibli as a serious contender in the world of cinema, not just animation. |
| **Distribution partnership with Disney** | In 1999, Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures acquired the North American distribution rights. Disney’s marketing muscle and established theatrical network gave *Princess Mononoke* a wide release in the U.S. and Canada, exposing Ghibli’s work to millions who had never seen a Japanese animated feature before. |
| **Foundation for future releases** | The success of *Princess Mononoke* paved the way for *Spirited Away* (2001) to secure a similar partnership with Disney, leading to its historic Oscar win in 2003. Subsequent titles (*Howl’s Moving Castle*, *Ponyo*, etc.) benefited from the distribution infrastructure and brand recognition built during this period. |
| **Cultivation of a global fanbase** | The film’s themes—environmentalism, spirituality, complex characters—resonated across cultures. Its availability on home video, streaming platforms, and in specialty cinemas created a dedicated international following that grew with each new release. |

In short, *Princess Mononoke*’s domestic box‑office triumph and critical success convinced major distributors (most notably Disney) that Ghibli’s films were commercially viable abroad. That partnership opened the door to wide releases, marketing campaigns, and award circuits outside Japan, turning Ghibli from a national treasure into a globally recognized powerhouse of animation.
